title: New in Chicago
premise: Find your bearings, a bed and a practical next step on an imagined first day in town.

opening.text:
JAUNT: NEW IN CHICAGO. Your first morning in a town incorporated less than two years ago, when it had twenty-eight legal voters; this summer it has two newspapers, a land office and more strangers than beds. You are one of them.

Five stops, from the forks to South Water Street: a landmark to steer by, the old mail corner, the store everyone uses, a map of the town, and a bed for tonight, if one can be had. The houses of 1834 'were always full', and full meant three in a bed.

stops.text: Begin outside the Sauganash. Recalling 1831, Juliette Kinzie described a white two-storey house with blue shutters. Moses and Kirkland call it 'the most attractive hostlery the city possessed', and its landlord Mark Beaubien, 'with his merry fiddle, the most popular of hosts'. Every newcomer learns this corner first.
stops.narrative: Let that landmark be your starting point. You are finding your bearings; the town is finding room for you.

stops.text: This is the old mail corner. John S. C. Hogan, made postmaster in 1832, handed out letters 'in a room partitioned off for that purpose' in his log store. Andreas says the office moved about July 1834, and Hogan's card now offers goods 'one door below the Post Office'. Ask for your letters there, not here.
stops.narrative: Keep the old corner as a landmark on your route; do not mistake it for the town’s current mail counter.

stops.text: At Peck's store, on South Water at LaSalle, note a supply shop. It was the village's first two-storey frame, built of black walnut lumber 'brought from Detroit by a boat'. His own advertisements list dry goods, hardware, groceries, crockery, boots, shoes and hats. Upstairs, Peck gave the young minister Jeremiah Porter 'a lodging place and study'.
stops.narrative: Remember where the everyday things are sold.

stops.text: This building keeps the Democrat’s first address; by May 1835 the paper printed over Jones and King’s hardware store. That spring it still ran Kinzie and Forsyth’s notice of lithographed town maps, also to be had at the paper’s office.
stops.narrative: A town map is a practical next step. Read the notice.

stops.text: Finish at Brown's boarding house. Andreas names Mrs Rufus Brown as a boarding-house keeper and places her log house behind Peck's store, which you passed a block ago. Andreas says the houses of 1834 'were always full; and full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides.' A spot on the floor counts as a bed.

choices.label: Board by the week
choices.consequence: Your route note favours cost: one arrangement for the whole stay.

choices.label: A bed close to the stores
choices.consequence: Your route note favours convenience: Peck’s is just in front.

stops.narrative: Choose what matters more on a first day: cost or convenience.

legs.note: A short step: the Sauganash and Hogan’s old log store both stand by the forks.
legs.story: Follow the route toward the old mail corner; your first day is taking shape.

legs.note: The long leg: east along South Water Street, about three hundred metres, to the stores at LaSalle.
legs.story: Ride the river street toward the stores and find where everyday things are sold.

legs.note: One block on along South Water, to the Democrat’s first corner at Clark.
legs.story: Look for news, and for something to find your way by.

legs.note: Back a block, to the house Andreas places behind Peck’s store.
legs.story: With a map in mind, think about where to sleep tonight.

endings.text: Your route note ends with weekly board behind Peck's. Cost decided. You may share the floor, but you have an address in the fastest-growing town in the West.
Your route note ends with a bed a few steps from the stores. Convenience decided, and tomorrow starts close to everything.
You have a few names and corners to connect. Every old settler in this town started exactly here: new, muddy and looking for a bed.

keepsake.title: Finding Your Feet
keepsake.text: A fictional route note linking five first-day landmarks, a town map notice and a place to sleep.

evidence.text: Kinzie describes the Sauganash in 1831 as a white two-storey building with blue shutters.
evidence.locator: Chapter XVII, Chicago in 1831; description of Mark Beaubien’s newly completed house.

evidence.text: Hogan’s store housed the post office in 1833; the office moved to Franklin and South Water about July 1834.
evidence.locator: Vol. 1, printed pp. 139–140, Postal Affairs; removal paragraph on p. 140.

evidence.text: Jeremiah Porter lodged in the unfinished loft of Peck’s two-storey store in May 1833.
evidence.locator: Vol. 1, printed p. 303, Jeremiah Porter biography; May 1833 arrival and temporary lodging.

evidence.text: P. F. W. Peck advertised from the corner of LaSalle and South Water streets a stock of dry goods, hardware, groceries, crockery, boots and shoes, and hats.
evidence.locator: 3 Dec 1833, p. 3, col. 4 (Peck’s standing card, run to 10 Dec 1834); 2 July 1834, p. 4, col. 4 (‘a full stock of fresh GOODS’). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: The Democrat’s first issue places its office at South Water and Clark; by 20 May 1835 its colophon places it over Jones and King’s hardware store.
evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833, imprint; 20 May 1835, p. 4, col. 6, colophon (transcription lines 4177–4180).

evidence.text: Kinzie & Forsyth advertised lithographic maps of the town of Chicago, including the School Section, Kinzie’s Addition and Wabansia, adding that they could also be found at the office of the Chicago Democrat. The notice, dated 18 June 1834, was still running in June 1835.
evidence.locator: ‘Town Maps’ notice dated 18 June 1834: 20 May 1835, p. 3, col. 6 (transcription lines 2918–2928); 10 June 1835, p. 4, col. 3 (lines 3496–3504). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: Andreas names Mrs Rufus Brown as a boarding-house keeper in his account of 1833, and places Brown’s log house behind Peck’s store.
evidence.locator: Vol. 1, printed p. 132, boarding-house paragraph; p. 303, Jeremiah Porter biography.

evidence.text: When the town was incorporated in August 1833, 'thirteen votes were cast by the twenty-eight legal electors', twelve in favour and one, Russel E. Heacock's, against.
evidence.locator: p. 91, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12319-12325 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Moses and Kirkland call the Sauganash 'the most attractive hostlery the city possessed', and its genial landlord, 'with his merry fiddle, the most popular of hosts'.
evidence.locator: p. 87, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 11879-11886 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: John S. C. Hogan was appointed postmaster on 2 November 1832 and handed out the mail 'in a room partitioned off for that purpose' from his log storehouse, 45 by 18 feet, where Lake and South Water streets meet.
evidence.locator: p. 90, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12197-12206 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: P. F. W. Peck's two-storey frame store, the first in the village, was built of lumber 'sawed from black walnut trees' and 'brought from Detroit by a boat'; his goods moved into it in the fall of 1831.
evidence.locator: p. 570, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 99826-99842 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Peck gave the Rev. Jeremiah Porter 'a lodging place and study in the second story of his store building', and there was held 'one of the earliest Sunday-schools organized in the town'.
evidence.locator: p. 571, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 99868-99876 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Immigration in 1833 'assumed proportions surpassing all expectation'; the year's arrivals included John Dean Caton, Silas B. Cobb, Asahel Pierce and the Rev. Jeremiah Porter, and about 165 frame buildings went up.
evidence.locator: p. 90, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12227-12245 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: J. S. C. Hogan's advertisement, dated 30 July 1834 and still printed on 27 May 1835, offers dry goods, groceries, hardware, crockery and glass ware at his store in South Water Street, one door below the Post Office.
evidence.locator: 27 May 1835 (Vol. II No. 6), p. 3, col. 5, Hogan's card. Transcription-mediated reading; the same card runs in the issues of 20 May to 1 July 1835.

evidence.text: The houses of 1834 were always full; and full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides.
evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1 on the houses of 1834, quoted on the card brown_mrs_rufus (data/residents/households/hh_brown_rufus.json).

evidence.text: The early lodging and store sites are treated as orientation stops in the July 1835 reconstruction; earlier descriptions do not prove a vacancy or a transaction that day.
evidence.reasoning: Uses the existing scene-date structure phases and their continuity arguments. Stop labels are building identities, not proof of continuing tenancies; Peck’s card and the map notice date their trades, not 1 July 1835. Brown’s absolute placement is reconstructed; the other four positions are inferred.

evidence.text: The visitor’s first-day errand, the reading of the map notice, the boarding choice, the cost-or-convenience preference, the endings, the route note, the ride on horseback (the recommended mode), timing inputs and the Finding Your Feet keepsake are invented connective narrative, not historical events.
